title: Applied Kinetics targets the equipment delays holding up data centers
summary: Applied Kinetics targets the equipment delays holding up data centers
body_markdown:
[Applied Kinetics](https://appliedkinetics.ai/) is quoting seven weeks to build and test pad-mount transformers, an attempt to shorten a wait that can hold up a data center long after its developers have lined up land and financing. The startup combines a manufacturing network with software agents that review specifications and track orders through production and delivery.


The seven-week figure is a company quote, not a verified delivery record. In its launch announcement, Applied Kinetics compares it with waits of up to 65 weeks on the open market. The distinction matters for equipment ordered to a particular project’s requirements: a quoted build-and-test interval is not necessarily the same as the complete time to installation and service.


The company supplies transformers, switchgear, generators and cooling systems. Its role extends beyond finding an available factory. Applied Kinetics says it manages design approvals, production, export arrangements, customs, freight and post-delivery support, with independent quality assurance near the destination site.


Its scheduling approach uses manufacturers across the United States, Europe, Latin America and Asia-Pacific. Instead of putting every order into one factory’s queue, the company says it assigns work where production can start soonest. The website describes partner plants as its manufacturing base; it does not present those facilities as a set of factories the startup itself owns.


Software handles the coordination around that physical capacity. According to the launch, agents review project specifications, schedule production and follow milestones on the factory floor, flagging delays before they affect the customer’s timeline. Those functions address the administrative work between placing an order and receiving a piece of equipment.


[Watch Applied Kinetics’ original launch video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xtZgwxJMQeA) .


An example on the company’s website shows how that coordination is supposed to work. A supplier changes the dispatch timing for cooling equipment and attaches a revised technical document. The software connects the update with the installation schedule and purchasing record, then prepares a coordination brief for the project team. The team approves the next step.


Applied Kinetics also says customers can license the agents it built for its own operations. That adds a software offering to the equipment business, but the launch’s central proposition remains delivery: someone takes responsibility for the order from specification through arrival, rather than leaving a developer to reconcile several suppliers’ timelines.


The founders bring engineering backgrounds connected to the two halves of that proposition. CEO Rohit Naras studied computer engineering at Georgia Tech and worked on GPU telemetry at Crusoe. CTO Adhik Durga also studied computer engineering at Georgia Tech and previously built AI agents at IBM, according to the announcement and their public YC profiles. The company is in Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 batch.


The launch does not disclose completed order volumes or an independently verified on-time delivery rate. For a developer considering the service, the useful next conversation is specific: which equipment can be built to the required specification, when testing finishes, and when it actually reaches the site.
